title: Transactions in NoSQL
goal: By the end, you can say how much one transaction may cover in DynamoDB, MongoDB 9.0 and Cassandra, follow what each does when two transactions want the same account, explain why a Cassandra lightweight transaction needs four rounds of messages and where Accord stands in 2026, and tell when a better layout of the data beats a transaction.

warmup.q: Two payments from the family's account start at the same moment, each inside its own transaction in MongoDB, a database we'll meet in this lesson. Both read the balance, 100.00, and both try to take money off it. The second one tries while the first is still open. What happens to the second payment?
options: It waits until the first one finishes, then takes its money off the new balance
Its change fails at once with a write conflict, and the whole payment has to start again, from the read
Both changes go through, and the balance ends up wrong
It goes through, and the first payment is cancelled instead
warmup.why: MongoDB lets the first transaction to change a record win, and fails the second change at once with `WriteConflict`. It doesn't make it wait, because the second transaction's view of the data is already out of date: it read 100.00, which is no longer true. The fix is to cancel and run the whole payment again, reading the balance afresh. Waiting is the tempting answer, and it's what MongoDB does to a plain change made outside any transaction, as the second section shows. Both changes going through would lose one of them, which MongoDB's transactions prevent.

sections.h: DynamoDB: two-phase commit with no single coordinator to wait for
sections.body:
Let's start with the family's account. DynamoDB is Amazon's database service: you store items, records looked up by a key, and Amazon spreads them over many machines. Each slice of the data, called a partition, lives on its own storage node, a machine that holds it. The family's account is the item `A-1001`, with 100.00. The bike shop's account is `A-2002`, and the grocer's is `A-3003`. Each sits in a different partition, on a different machine.

So a payment from `A-1001` to `A-2002` is lesson 7's problem again. Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA found its weak spot in the coordinator, the program in charge. When it crashes, the participants wait, holding their locks (marks that stop anyone else from changing those records), until it comes back with its log. Every database that offers transactions across partitions meets the same problem. Each answers three questions in its own way: who decides, what a participant promises, and where the decision lives.

DynamoDB's answer starts with one request. `TransactWriteItems` takes a list of changes and applies all of them or none. Say a debit on `A-1001`, a credit on `A-2002`, and a claim on an idempotency key, a unique id for this payment so that a repeat does nothing. DynamoDB single-table design and transactions ran exactly this. It cost two writes per item, and it could fail with `TransactionConflict`. The limits are fixed: up to 100 changes to distinct items, 4 MB in all, in one Amazon account and one Region. A Region is one of Amazon's areas of data centres, such as Ireland. A single-item read sees the transaction all or nothing. But `Query` and `Scan`, which read many items, can see some of its items changed and others not. A client token, an id you send with the request, makes a retry safe for 10 minutes.

How does it work? Amazon's engineers described it in a 2023 paper at USENIX ATC, a computer systems conference. It's lesson 7's protocol with the weak spot removed. Amazon runs a whole fleet of coordinators, and any of them can take any transaction. The one that takes it stamps it with a timestamp from its own clock.

Phase one is prepare. A storage node accepts a prepare only if three things hold. The item's condition must be true, such as "balance at least 30.00". The timestamp must be newer than the item's last write. And no other transaction may be in flight on the item. That last rule replaces waiting for locks. A held item makes the node say no at once, and one no cancels the whole transaction. Then the coordinator records its decision in a **ledger**, which is itself a DynamoDB table with copies on several machines. Only then does it send the commits. If a coordinator dies, a recovery manager that scans the ledger hands its transaction to another coordinator, which finishes it. Nobody waits for one particular machine to come back, and no item stays held for long.

A travel agent booking a flight and a hotel for one trip works much the same way. She asks each to hold a booking, and a held seat can't go to anyone else. When both are held, she writes "confirmed" in the file and tells both. DynamoDB's twist is that a seat already held for another trip makes the airline say no at once, with no waiting list. And the file sits in a shared cabinet, where any colleague can finish the booking if she goes home sick. The hold is the prepare, the file is the ledger, and the colleague is a new coordinator. The picture breaks on time: a hold lasts a day, and here it all happens in milliseconds.

**Across machines, everyone promises first, one decision is written where a crash can't erase it, and only then does anything change.** The facts from the DynamoDB lesson fall out of this. Two writes per item are the two rounds, and `TransactionConflict` is a rejected prepare. The paper also describes a shortcut: when all the items sit in one partition, one node can check and write everything in a single round.

DynamoDB keeps waiting out by saying no. Next, MongoDB, which does it with snapshots.

try.title: Run the two-phase protocol, with a conflict and a crash
steps: DynamoDB Local, the free copy of DynamoDB that runs on a laptop, runs transactions one at a time, so it can't show a conflict: sent 20 three-item payments at once out of one account, it committed all 20 on the first try. sections.h: MongoDB: each transaction reads a snapshot, and the first writer wins
sections.body:
MongoDB is a database that stores each record as a document, a set of named fields much like a JSON object (the text format web programs use to send data). Document stores with MongoDB kept a payment and its refunds in one document. Then one guarded `updateOne`, a change whose filter checks a condition first, could check and change them together. When the rule spans documents, say a payment that changes two account documents and adds a ledger document, MongoDB has multi-document transactions.

They run only on a replica set, a group of servers that keep copies of the same data. They also run on a sharded cluster, where the data is split across several such groups, but not on a lone server. That's why this track's lab files run even one MongoDB server as a replica set of one, named `rs0`.

Inside a MongoDB transaction you can read, decide in your own code, and write, as you would in PostgreSQL. So how does MongoDB keep two transactions apart? Let's build it up.

The first version locks everything a transaction reads, until it commits. That's two-phase locking, which holds every lock until commit, from Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI (lesson 5). It's correct, but a long report would block every payment it touched.

The second version is what MongoDB does for reads. Each transaction reads from a **snapshot**: the data as it was committed when the transaction started. To make this work, the storage engine, the part of the database that keeps data on disk, holds on to old versions. That's the idea of MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM (lesson 4). Reads never wait, and they never make anyone else wait.

Writes still need a rule. If two transactions change the same document, the second change fails at once with `WriteConflict`. The first writer wins, and nobody waits. The error carries a label, `TransientTransactionError`, which means: cancel and run the whole transaction again. Retrying only the failed change would be wrong, because the transaction's snapshot no longer matches the data. In the Try it, tx2 fails, then retries on a new snapshot that sees tx1's debit, and its own condition turns out false.

MongoDB's library for Java programs (its driver) has `session.withTransaction { }`, which runs this loop for you. It reruns the block on `TransientTransactionError`, retries only the commit on `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` (the server may or may not have committed), and gives up after 120 seconds. The lab writes the same loop by hand, so you know what it does.

Four limits matter in practice. First, a plain change outside any transaction, to a document an open transaction has changed, waits until that transaction ends. Second, a transaction must finish within `transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`, 60 seconds by default, or a cleanup task cancels it. Third, MongoDB 9.0 lets clients keep at most 10,000 transactions open at once (`maxConcurrentMultiDocumentTransactions`). Past that, a new one fails with `TooManyOpenTransactions`, so slow transactions can't pile up without end. Fourth, a snapshot isn't serializable, the promise that transactions behave as if they ran one at a time. Two transactions that read the same two balances and each change a different one don't conflict: that's the write skew of Write skew and phantoms (lesson 3). Keep the rule inside the change itself, with guarded updates.

Two more facts. On a sharded cluster, a transaction that writes to several groups commits with lesson 7's two-phase commit, with one group as coordinator. That costs extra round trips, each one a message out and its answer back. And Jepsen, a project that tests databases for lost data under faults, found in 2020 that MongoDB 4.2.6's transactions were weaker than their settings suggested. Its advice still holds: set `readConcern: "snapshot"` and `writeConcern: "majority"` on every transaction yourself. They mean "read one consistent snapshot" and "count a commit as done only once most of the replica set has it".

MongoDB keeps the waiting out with snapshots and a first-writer rule. Cassandra goes further: it has no leader at all. Next, we'll see how its copies agree on anything.

steps: From the `labs` folder, start MongoDB 9.0 as a replica set of one: `docker compose -f env/mongo.yml up -d --wait`. Docker runs it in a container, a small separate machine on your laptop.

Read the script below. Predict what tx2's debit prints, what a read from outside the transactions sees before tx1 commits, and what tx2 sees when it retries. The last part sleeps for 12 seconds on purpose.
Run it with mongosh, MongoDB's shell: `docker compose -f env/mongo.yml exec mongo mongosh sfz --quiet /sfz/nosql-10-transactions.js`. Then stop MongoDB: `docker compose -f env/mongo.yml down -v`.

try.expect:
```text
tx1 reads A-1001: 10000
tx2 reads A-1001: 10000
tx1 debit 3000: 1
tx2 debit 8000: WriteConflict ["TransientTransactionError"]
outside, before tx1 commits: 10000
outside, after tx1 commits: 7000
tx2 retry reads A-1001: 7000
tx2 retry debit 8000: 0
outside write: MaxTimeMSExpired after 2028 ms
transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds: 60
commit after 12 s: NoSuchTransaction
A-1001 at the end: 7000
```

Both transactions read 10000 from their snapshots. tx1 writes first, so tx2's write fails at once with `WriteConflict` and the label `TransientTransactionError`. From outside, nobody sees tx1's debit until it commits. tx2's retry is a new transaction with a new snapshot: it sees 7000, and its guarded debit of 8000 changes nothing. The plain change outside a transaction waited for tx1 until its 2-second `maxTimeMS` ran out. With the limit set to 5 seconds, the server's cleanup cancelled the transaction that slept 12. So its commit finds `NoSuchTransaction`, its debit never happened, and `A-1001` is still 7000.

sections.h: Cassandra: copies of one partition agree on one value with Paxos
sections.body:
Cassandra is a database that spreads rows over many machines with no leader. Every copy of a partition, called a replica, takes writes, and any node can take a client's request and coordinate it. Wide-column stores with Cassandra claimed an idempotency key with `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS`, which writes the row only if no row with that key exists yet. Leaderless replication: quorums, hinted handoff and read repair showed why plain quorums can't do that. A quorum is a majority of the replicas, two of three. Two coordinators both read "no row" at `QUORUM`, and both write. Then the rule last write wins keeps the one with the later timestamp, without telling the other. Two payments both think they claimed the key.

A check-then-write like this is called compare-and-set. It needs the replicas to agree on one order before anyone writes. With no leader to decide, Cassandra runs Paxos, a consensus protocol by Leslie Lamport: rules by which several machines agree on one value, even when some of them crash. It runs Paxos for that one partition only. Consensus with Raft, in the Consistency and consensus track, builds a close relative. Here we build only as much Paxos as one partition needs.

Let's build it from the race. The first version stamps each attempt with a ballot, a number that only grows, and asks the replicas to promise to refuse anything lower. Once a majority has promised ballot 2, an attempt still holding ballot 1 is refused when it tries to write. Any two majorities of three share at least one replica, so two attempts can't both hold a majority's promise.

That isn't enough. Say attempt 1 got its value accepted by one replica, and then its coordinator died. Attempt 2 can't tell whether that value was already chosen by a majority. So every promise also reports any value the replica accepted but never saw committed. And Paxos's one rule says the newcomer must **finish that value before proposing its own**. The stepper shows it.

Cassandra calls this compare-and-set a lightweight transaction (LWT). It costs four round trips to a majority of replicas, and each one shows in the Try it's trace, Cassandra's record of what it did for one request:

1. Prepare and promise: "Promising ballot".
2. Read the current row and check the `IF`: "Reading existing values for CAS precondition".
3. Propose and accept: "Accepting proposal".
4. Commit, which writes the row into the table: "Committing proposal".

A plain write is one round trip. The Paxos state lives in a table of its own, `system.paxos`. That's why the trace says "Adding to paxos memtable": a memtable is the in-memory table where Cassandra collects new writes before they go to disk. If the condition is false, you get `[applied] = False` and the current row. Each Cassandra request names a consistency level, how many replicas must answer, such as `QUORUM`. The Paxos phases use a serial level, `SERIAL`, or `LOCAL_SERIAL` for a majority inside one data centre. A read at `SERIAL` goes through Paxos too, so it sees every applied LWT.

The costs are easy to list. Each LWT waits for four majority round trips. Two clients racing on one partition can keep beating each other's ballots, until one gives up after `cas_contention_timeout`, 1 second in the 5.0.9 settings file, `cassandra.yaml`. Cassandra 4.1 added Paxos v2, which needs two round trips for a write, but 5.0.9 still ships v1 as the default. And it covers one partition only: a batch of writes with an `IF` condition can't span partitions.

One partition at a time is a tight fit for payments between accounts. Next, we'll meet Cassandra's answer for many partitions, and the cases where no transaction at all is the better choice.

sections.h: Cassandra 6.0's Accord, and when a better data layout beats a transaction
sections.body:
Cassandra 6.0 adds Accord: transactions across partitions and tables, with no leader. They're strict serializable, the strongest of the usual promises. The result is as if the transactions ran one at a time, in an order that matches the clock on the wall. Any node can coordinate, and the common case needs one round trip of agreement.

As of November 2026 it's still alpha, an early test version. The Docker image `cassandra:6.0-alpha2` exists, but Apache's downloads page still lists 5.0 as the newest release, 6.0 has no release date, and the syntax may change. Accord also needs Cassandra's new cluster metadata service, which keeps the cluster's own list of members and settings agreed. An upgraded cluster switches it on with `nodetool cms initialize` (nodetool is Cassandra's admin command), a step that isn't easily undone. In the alpha, Accord is off until `accord.enabled: true` is set in `cassandra.yaml`, and each table opts in with `transactional_mode = 'full'`. A transaction reads with `LET`, decides with `IF ... THEN`, and writes, all between `BEGIN TRANSACTION` and `COMMIT TRANSACTION`. The Try it moves 30.00 between two partitions of two tables in one statement. Treat it as the direction Cassandra is going, not something to build payments on yet.

Databases built for transactions from the start take another road. Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL, in the Consistency and consensus track, shows how Spanner and CockroachDB run lesson 7's two-phase commit over participants whose copies agree through consensus.

Now the harder question: when should you not use a transaction at all? Every tool in this lesson charges something. DynamoDB bills two writes per item and cancels when two transactions meet. MongoDB cancels on write conflicts and after 60 seconds. A Cassandra LWT costs four round trips per write. And between two separate programs, each with its own database, which is where many payments really run, there's no shared transaction at all.

A better layout of the data often removes the need:

- Put what must change together into one item or document. In Document stores with MongoDB, keeping the refunds inside the payment's own document made the refund rule one guarded update.
- Make one conditional write do the job. Claiming an idempotency key is one put with `attribute_not_exists` in DynamoDB, or one `IF NOT EXISTS` in Cassandra, with no transaction.
- Split a payment between two accounts into steps that each touch one partition. Let a workflow engine, a program that drives a job of several steps to the end through crashes, run them. Debit `A-1001` and record the pending payment in `A-1001`'s own document. Then credit `A-2002`, guarded so a repeat does nothing. Then mark it done. If the credit can never succeed, a compensating step refunds the debit. That's lesson 7's saga. The money is visibly "in flight" for a moment, and a check that runs every night can find any payment that got stuck.

**Use the smallest thing that keeps the rule.** When the business already treats a payment between two accounts as pending, use the saga. Run it with a workflow engine like the ones in Durable execution: workflows that survive crashes. Use a transaction when the rule needs one step that can't be split, such as an idempotency claim and the payment it guards. And keep that transaction inside one partition or one document when you can.

compare.note: MongoDB runs a conversation. The session opens a snapshot, your Kotlin code reads and decides, and the server checks for write conflicts as the writes arrive. That freedom costs a retry loop around your own code, which `withTransaction` provides. Accord takes the whole transaction as one statement: reads go in `LET`, decisions in `IF`, and the cluster puts it in order against every other transaction before running it, so there's no conflict for your code to retry. DynamoDB's `TransactWriteItems` sits between them: one request, with no reads at all, only conditions. Because MongoDB lets your code decide between the read and the write, keep the condition in the update's filter as well, as the Kotlin does. The other two decide inside the database.

worked.title: A payment between two accounts without a cross-partition transaction

steps.say: Start from the rule and from what the business already accepts. A payment may show as pending for a few seconds. It must never move money twice, or lose it. The two accounts are two MongoDB documents, perhaps in two different groups of servers (shards).
steps.code:
transfer txf-k-1: 30.00 from A-1001 to A-2002
must hold:  never debited twice, never credited twice, never debited without a credit in the end
may happen: A-1001 shows the debit a moment before A-2002 shows the credit

steps.say: Step 1 is one all-or-nothing write on `A-1001`'s document: debit it and record the pending payment inside it. The filter checks the balance and that this payment's id isn't recorded yet, so a retry changes nothing.
steps.code:
db.accounts.updateOne(
  { _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: { $gte: 3000 }, "pending.id": { $ne: "txf-k-1" } },
  { $inc: { balanceMinor: -3000 },
    $push: { pending: { id: "txf-k-1", to: "A-2002", amountMinor: 3000 } } })
// modifiedCount 0: insufficient funds, or already done; read the document to tell which

steps.say: Step 2 is one all-or-nothing write on `A-2002`'s document: credit it, guarded by the same id, so running it twice credits once.
Step 3 closes the payment on `A-1001`: move it from `pending` to done. If step 2 can never succeed (the account was closed), the compensating step refunds `A-1001` instead, guarded the same way.

Something has to run steps 1 to 3 to the end, through crashes and restarts. That's a workflow engine, from Durable execution: workflows that survive crashes. Temporal, one such engine, would run the three writes as activities, the steps it retries until they answer. Each is safe to retry because each is guarded by the payment's id.
steps.code:
workflow transfer(txf-k-1):
  debit(A-1001)           activity, retried until it answers: done / insufficient
  credit(A-2002)          activity, retried; on permanent failure -> refund(A-1001)
  close(A-1001)           activity, retried
# no step ever holds two documents at once; a crash resumes at the next step

steps.say: Count what you traded. No transaction, so no write conflicts across accounts, no 60-second limit and no two-phase cost. In return: three writes instead of one commit, a moment when the money is visibly in flight, and a workflow engine you must run. For payments that's usually the right trade, because "pending" already exists in the business.
steps.code:
one transaction           saga of single-document writes
atomic across docs     yes                       no: in flight for a moment
conflicts / retries    the whole transaction     each step on its own
needs                  a replica set, 60 s max   a workflow engine (Temporal)
works across services  no                        yes

lab.title: Build Paxos compare-and-set, then a MongoDB transfer that survives write conflicts
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. `PaxosRegisterTest` needs no Docker. `MongoTransfersTest` starts a MongoDB replica set of one through Testcontainers, a library that starts Docker containers for tests (a few seconds, more the first time). All fourteen fail.

In `PaxosRegister.kt`, write `Acceptor.prepare` and `Acceptor.accept`. An acceptor is one replica's side of Paxos. Each method is three lines: compare the ballot with `promised`, then remember. The first two tests pass.

Write `compareAndSet` from its KDoc, the comment above it: check for a majority, prepare, finish any unfinished proposal and start again, read, propose, commit, and count round trips. Seven more pass, including the one where a crashed proposer's value must win, and the one that races 300 rounds of claims with lost messages.

In `MongoTransfers.kt`, write `transfer`: one session, then a loop of `startTransaction(options)`, the ledger insert, the guarded debit, the credit and the commit, retrying on `TransientTransactionError`. Five more pass. The conflict test holds a rival transaction open on `A-1001` for 300 ms and expects your first attempts to fail and a later one to succeed.
hints: `prepare`: `val p = promised; if (p != null && ballot <= p) return Promise.Rejected(p)`, then set `promised` and return `Promise.Ok(inProgress, committed)`. `accept` refuses only when `proposal.ballot < promised`. An equal ballot is fine: it comes from the proposer that prepared.

In `compareAndSet`, keep `var trips = 0` outside a `while (true)` loop, and `continue` after finishing someone else's proposal. Unfinished means an `inProgress` whose ballot is greater than the highest `committed` ballot among the `Ok` replies.
`highestPromise(replicas)` gives the ballot for `Contended`. `read(replicas)` is the read step.

MongoDB: every call takes the session first, as in `accounts.updateOne(session, filter, update)`. A duplicate ledger id is a `MongoWriteException` with `e.error.category == ErrorCategory.DUPLICATE_KEY`.

Catch `MongoException`, call `abortQuietly(session)`, and if `e.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL)`, sleep `backoff(attempt)` and loop. For the commit, loop while the error has `UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION_COMMIT_RESULT_LABEL`.

drill.title: The transaction retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. In Kotlin, write the loop that runs a MongoDB transaction body with the driver's core API: start a session, start a transaction with `snapshot` and `majority`, run `body(session)`, and commit. Retry the whole thing on `TransientTransactionError` (up to 10 attempts), and only the commit on `UnknownTransactionCommitResult`. Then say in one sentence why retrying only the failed statement is wrong.

recap: Lesson 7's rule holds here too: across partitions, every participant first promises, one decision is recorded where a crash can't erase it, then everything changes. One item, document or partition is all or nothing for free, because one machine owns it.

DynamoDB: up to 100 items and 4 MB in one Region. Coordinators prepare each item (condition, timestamp, nobody else in flight) and record decisions in a ledger table with copies on many machines. A rejected prepare is `TransactionConflict`; nothing waits, so retry with the same token. `Query` and `Scan` can see a transaction half done.

MongoDB: multi-document transactions read a snapshot and let the first writer of a document win. The loser gets `WriteConflict`, labelled `TransientTransactionError`, and reruns the whole transaction. 60 seconds by default, and 9.0 allows 10,000 open at once. Set `snapshot` and `majority` yourself.
Cassandra 5.0: a lightweight transaction runs Paxos on one partition, four round trips in the default v1 against one for a plain write. A newcomer must finish any accepted value it finds.

The limit: each of these charges for the guarantee, in writes, retries or round trips, and none spans two separate programs. Accord, Cassandra 6.0's transactions across partitions, is still alpha in November 2026. Before reaching for a transaction, try one document, one conditional write, or a saga of one-partition steps.

quiz.q: A `TransactWriteItems` that takes money from a busy shop's account fails with `TransactionCanceledException`, reason `TransactionConflict` on that debit. What happened inside DynamoDB?
options: The debit's condition was false
The transaction waited for a lock on the item and ran out of time
Another transaction was in flight on that item, so its storage node rejected the prepare, and the whole transaction was cancelled
The debit was applied, but the other items were not
quiz.why: A storage node accepts a prepare only if no other transaction is in flight on the item, and the condition and timestamp checks pass. One rejection cancels everything, and nothing was written. A false condition would say `ConditionalCheckFailed` instead. DynamoDB never queues one transaction behind another, so the right response is a retry after a short random wait, not a longer timeout.

quiz.q: A MongoDB transaction reads `A-1001` (100.00), decides to debit 80.00, and its `updateOne` fails with `WriteConflict`. A developer retries only that `updateOne`, inside the same session. What's wrong with that?
options: The transaction was cancelled and its snapshot is out of date; the read and the decision must be redone in a new transaction
Nothing: the update has a guard, so it's safe to retry
Write conflicts are permanent; the payment must be refused
The update must be retried outside the transaction
quiz.why: `TransientTransactionError` means "run the whole transaction again". Another transaction changed `A-1001` after this one's snapshot was taken, so the 100.00 it read is no longer true, and any decision based on it has to be made again on a new snapshot. Retrying outside the transaction would cut the debit loose from the credit and the ledger insert: one could happen without the others.

quiz.q: From Atomic commit across machines (lesson 7): a PostgreSQL participant whose coordinator died stays in doubt, holding its locks, until that coordinator returns with its log. What does DynamoDB do so that a crashed transaction coordinator doesn't leave items held?
options: It rolls back every prepared item after a fixed timeout
It has only one coordinator, copied to other machines with Paxos
Storage nodes ask each other for the outcome
Decisions go into a ledger that is itself a DynamoDB table with copies on many machines, and a recovery manager hands a stalled transaction to another coordinator, which finishes it
quiz.why: Classic two-phase commit keeps the decision on one coordinator's disk, and that's its weak spot. DynamoDB writes every decision to the copied ledger instead, so any coordinator can pick up a transaction whose coordinator died: commit it if it was decided, cancel it otherwise. A blind rollback after a timeout is the tempting answer, and it would break all or nothing for a transaction already decided commit.

quiz.q: During a lightweight transaction's prepare, one replica's promise reports a value it accepted under an older ballot and never saw committed. What must the new attempt do?
options: Ignore it: a value that was never committed doesn't count
Finish that value first (propose and commit it under its own ballot), then start its own operation again
Cancel and return an error to the client
Merge its own value with the old one
quiz.why: That value may already have been accepted by a majority, which would make it chosen, and the new attempt can't tell. Paxos's rule is to finish it. Ignoring it is the tempting answer, and it's the one that would let two different values win. The lab's test with a crashed proposer checks exactly this.

quiz.q: From Leaderless replication: quorums, hinted handoff and read repair: why can't QUORUM reads and QUORUM writes alone give you "claim this idempotency key only if nobody has"?
options: QUORUM reads don't see QUORUM writes
QUORUM writes are refused when the key exists
Two coordinators can both read "absent" before either writes; both writes succeed, and last write wins keeps one without telling the other
Idempotency keys need ALL, not QUORUM
quiz.why: With R + W > N (the replicas a read waits for, plus those a write waits for, is more than the total), every read overlaps every write that finished before it. But nothing puts a read and a write from two different clients in order. Both claims read before either wrote, so both saw no row. Both writes are then acknowledged, and timestamps settle the outcome silently. A lightweight transaction adds the missing agreement on order, with Paxos.

flashcards.front: What are the limits of one DynamoDB transaction?
flashcards.back: Up to 100 changes on distinct items, 4 MB in all, one account and one Region. `Query`, `Scan` and `BatchGetItem` may see it half applied.

flashcards.front: When does a DynamoDB storage node reject a transaction's prepare?
flashcards.back: When a condition fails, the item would break a limit, the transaction's timestamp isn't newer than the item's last write, or another transaction is in flight on the item (`TransactionConflict`).

flashcards.front: What does `TransientTransactionError` tell your MongoDB code?
flashcards.back: Cancel and run the whole transaction again, reads included, on a new snapshot. A write conflict is the usual cause.

flashcards.front: What limits does MongoDB put on transactions?
flashcards.back: 60 seconds by default (`transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`), after which a cleanup task cancels it; and since 9.0, at most 10,000 open at once (`TooManyOpenTransactions`).

flashcards.front: The four round trips of a Cassandra lightweight transaction (Paxos v1)?
flashcards.back: Prepare and promise, read (check the IF), propose and accept, commit. Each waits for a majority of replicas.

flashcards.front: Paxos's one rule for a new attempt?
flashcards.back: If a promise reports an accepted value newer than the last commit, finish that value before proposing your own.

flashcards.front: What is Accord, and can you build on it today?
flashcards.back: Cassandra 6.0's transactions across partitions and tables (`BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT TRANSACTION`), strict serializable. 6.0 is alpha in November 2026: not yet.

terms.plain: Lesson 7's protocol: every participant prepares and promises, one decision is written durably, then all commit or cancel.
The program that runs a transaction across machines and decides its outcome. DynamoDB keeps a fleet of them and a ledger of their decisions.
Each transaction reads the data as it was committed when it started. Reads never wait; two writers of one item conflict. Write skew is still possible.
Two open transactions changing the same document. MongoDB fails the second change at once and labels the error `TransientTransactionError`.
A consensus protocol: replicas promise ballots and accept proposals so that only one value is chosen, even through crashes and races.
The ever-growing number a Paxos attempt carries; replicas refuse anything lower than what they promised. Cassandra uses a time-based UUID.
Cassandra's compare-and-set on one partition, `IF NOT EXISTS` or `IF col = ...`, run with Paxos. The reply's `[applied]` says whether it happened.
A long job made of local all-or-nothing steps, each with a compensating step, driven to the end by a workflow engine instead of one transaction.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "NoSQL databases have transactions now, so we can wrap the payment in one and stop worrying." Explain what a transaction across partitions has to do, what DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cassandra each do when two writers collide, and when you'd lay out the payment differently.
explain_back.answer: Across partitions no single machine can make the change all or nothing, so every store does a version of the same thing. Each participant first promises: DynamoDB holds the item after a successful prepare, and Paxos replicas promise a ballot. One decision is recorded where a crash can't lose it: DynamoDB's ledger, or a majority of Paxos replicas. Only then does data change. Collisions are where they differ. DynamoDB rejects the second transaction's prepare and cancels it with TransactionConflict, and our code retries after a short random wait. MongoDB gives each transaction a snapshot and fails the second writer of a document with WriteConflict, labelled TransientTransactionError, so we rerun the whole transaction, reads included; it also cancels anything older than 60 seconds. Cassandra only offers compare-and-set on one partition, a lightweight transaction that costs four Paxos round trips, and Accord, its transactions across partitions, is still alpha in 6.0. So transactions exist, but they cost writes, retries and time, and none spans two separate programs. For a payment between two accounts I'd rather do two single-document conditional writes keyed by the payment id, a debit that records the pending payment and a credit that can't happen twice, driven by a workflow engine such as Temporal, with a compensating refund. I'd keep a transaction for things that must be one step, like an idempotency claim and the payment it guards, ideally inside one partition.

deeper.body:
**More fine print in DynamoDB.** In a global table, which keeps copies of a table in several Regions, a transaction is all or nothing only in the Region where you wrote it. DynamoDB Streams, the feed of changes that other programs can read, doesn't keep a transaction's changes together either: a reader of the stream shouldn't assume it sees a whole transaction at once.

**Tricks from the DynamoDB paper.** A plain read isn't blocked by a prepared transaction: a `GetItem` returns the last committed value and is put in order before the pending transaction. A plain `PutItem` with no condition can even be put in order before a prepared transaction, because the transaction's later write will overwrite it anyway. `TransactGetItems` writes nothing: it reads every item with its log sequence number, reads them again, and succeeds only if nothing changed in between. And deleted items are tracked with one maximum-delete timestamp per partition rather than a marker per item, which now and then cancels a transaction that could have run.

**Three answers to lesson 7's in-doubt problem.** Classic two-phase commit keeps the decision on one coordinator's disk, so its participants wait when it dies. DynamoDB keeps the decision in a copied ledger and lets any coordinator finish it. Google Spanner goes further: every participant is itself a Paxos group, so a participant never disappears either. Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL takes that apart.

**Paxos v2.** Cassandra's Paxos v2 (4.1 and later) cuts a write to two round trips, roughly by combining the read with the prepare, and the commit with the next operation's prepare. The `cassandra.yaml` of 5.0.9 lists the variants with their round trips: v1 "Expect 4RTs for a write and 3RTs for a read", v2 "Expect 2RTs for a write, and either 1RT or 2RT for a read". To switch, run a full repair on every node, set `paxos_variant: v2` and restart one node at a time; going back works the same way.

**Accord's fast path.** Accord's "one round trip in the common case" holds when the replicas agree on the transaction's place in the order straight away. When concurrent transactions disagree, it falls back to a slower path. That's the same shape as Paxos with a stable leader, and the reason contention costs time in every one of these systems.

**One more paper.** Read Jepsen's MongoDB 4.2.6 report end to end. It shows how a test harness finds lost writes and read skew, and why a database's defaults and its documentation matter as much as its protocol.

opening:
Picture a family sharing one account in a payments app. Two of them pay at the same second: one for groceries, one for a bike repair. There's enough for both. One payment goes through. The other comes back at once with an error that says, "someone else is busy with this account, try again".

It's easy to expect the second payment to wait its turn, as people queue at a counter, because waiting feels fair and safe. It's also easy to think a transaction works the same in every database: wrap the changes in one, and the database sorts out the rest.

In Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA, PostgreSQL made writers wait behind a prepared transaction as long as its coordinator was gone. In this lesson, we'll take three databases built to spread data over many machines, DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cassandra. We'll collide two transactions in each, see who decides and who waits, and find when a better layout of the data does the job instead. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a family whose second payment came back at once with "try again". DynamoDB and MongoDB both refuse to make one transaction wait for another, so the loser hears no straight away and starts again with a fresh look at the balance.

Start MongoDB from this lesson's Try it and run `db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds: 1 })`. That 60 is how many seconds any transaction may live.

That ends the Transactions track. Every protocol in it had to cope with a machine that went quiet and might be dead or only slow. Next, in the Faults, time and truth track, we'll look at that silence itself: when a request gets no answer, what could have happened, and why the sender can't tell which.
